abstract: Immediately following a blood meal, the female tick must locate conditions that allow successful egg development. A contributing factor is that conditions must be sufficiently moist to prevent egg dehydration. Previous studies show that humidity detection occurs through the forelegs and that interference with this process leads to tick mortality; however, this effect has not been examined in fed tick stages. Here, we show that female ticks exhibit a distinct attraction to higher humidity, directing them to locations where they arrest and subsequently deposit eggs. Interference with humidity detection caused fed females to deposit eggs at RHs below the optimal range for egg viability. Evaluation of tick egg viability at cluster sizes of 1, 5, 50, and naturally laid clusters (over 500 eggs) in relation to varying relative humidities reveals that depositing clusters of eggs under higher humidity conditions is critical for viability (Egg viability remained low below 85% RH but increased substantially at higher humidity levels). We found that application of the repellent DEET (N,N-diethyl-meta-toluamide) disrupted this behavior. Field validation shows a drastic reduction in surviving larvae when females cannot detect humidity (mechanical or chemical inhibition) during egg deposition. These studies confirm that fed female ticks must detect a humid site after detachment from the host to ensure egg viability, and that disrupting this process could be an effective tick control strategy.
